caption:
बाप रे! इस ब्लॉकबस्टर चीनी फिल्म ने कमाल कर दिया है जो आज तक कोई Disney या Pixar नहीं कर पाया! 😱🔥

Box Office Mojo की रिपोर्ट के मुताबिक, Ne Zha 2 इतिहास की पहली ऐसी animated film बन गई है जिसने $2 billion का आंकड़ा पार किया और कुल $2.27 billion की कमाई की! 💰✨

फरवरी 2025 में रिलीज होने के कुछ ही हफ्तों बाद इसने Pixar की Inside Out 2 को पीछे छोड़ दिया था। 📈

Beijing Review के अनुसार, इस 144 मिनट की फिल्म को बनाने में 138 कंपनियों के 4000 से ज्यादा animators को 5 साल का वक्त लगा था। 🎬

Director Yang Yu (जिन्हें Jiaozi कहा जाता है) ने quality से समझौता करने के बजाय schedule बढ़ाना बेहतर समझा। ⏱️

फिल्म में 1900 special effects shots और 10,000 से ज्यादा effects elements थे, जहां सिर्फ एक 10-second sequence को ठीक करने में एक साल से ज्यादा लग गया। 🤯

Forbes के मुताबिक, A24 ने इसे US release हैंडल किया और इसे modern animation में milestone बताया। 🌟

Deadline की रिपोर्ट के मुताबिक, film के repeat viewings word of mouth, family, growing up और justice जैसी themes की वजह से हुए। 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦

NBC News के अनुसार, यह film 29 January 2025 को Lunar New Year के मौके पर रिलीज हुई थी। 🏮

France 24 के मुताबिक, AFP से बात करते हुए एक युवा चीनी नागरिक ने कहा कि उसे एक चीनी व्यक्ति होने पर गर्व महसूस हुआ। 🇨🇳

हालांकि Deadline ने चेतावनी दी थी कि patriotic duty शायद वो वजह नहीं थी जिससे लोगों ने tickets खरीदे, बल्कि quality और emotional pull ने काम किया। ❤️

लेकिन क्या आपने कभी सोचा था कि Hollywood के बिना भी कोई animated movie इतनी बड़ी हिट बन सकती है? नीचे comments में बताओ! 👇

ctx.text:
A Chinese film about a rebellious demon child has done what no Disney or Pixar blockbuster could. Ne Zha 2 became the first animated film in history to pass the $2 billion mark, finishing with about $2.27 billion , per Box Office Mojo . It overtook Pixar’s Inside Out 2 ( $1.6 billion ) as the highest-grossing animated film ever in February 2025, just weeks after it opened.
But how did this happen? Here are three things that help explain how it got there.
Well, the first is just plain, stubborn craftsmanship. According to Beijing Review , more than 4,000 animators from 138 companies spent five years on the 144-minute film. Director Yang Yu, who goes by Jiaozi, refused to rush it. The team first expected to finish in three to four years, but he chose to “extend the schedule rather than compromise on quality.”
The film ended up with 1,900 special effects shots and over 10,000 effects elements. A single 10-second sequence took more than a year to get right. Western critics took notice of it as well, as The New York Times called it a “testament to the level of artistry in the Chinese animation industry right now.” A24, which handled the US release, called it a “milestone in modern animation,” per Forbes .
Truth be told, the second reason is that the story feels both old and new at once. The film is based on a 16th-century novel, but it turns a folk tale into something more personal. The writers took the original myth’s “filial conflict” and reshaped it into a story about fighting fate to change your own destiny, and that struck a chord with Gen Z around the world.
The first film was about defying fate. But the sequel goes further and pushes back on institutions and the way things are, arguing that good and evil are not decided by race or where you come from. Deadline found that repeat viewings came from word of mouth and themes like family, growing up, a parent’s sacrifice, and the search for justice.
The third reason is timing and national pride. The film opened on January 29, 2025, right at the start of Lunar New Year, one of the biggest moviegoing periods of the year. It landed in a market where the 2024 box office was 34% below its pre-Covid peak, per NBC News . Over that holiday, average cinema occupancy went above 40%, compared with a national average of 5.8% in 2024.
The film also caught a bigger mood. Audiences were proud that it was made entirely in China, starting from the director to the special effects teams. As per France 24 , one young Chinese national, told AFP, “I felt a deep sense of pride as a Chinese person.” Even Deadline warned that “patriotic duty” probably wasn’t what drove most people to buy tickets. Its view was that quality and emotional pull did the job.
The numbers show just how much of the success happened at home. More than 99% of its early earnings came from mainland China, unlike Hollywood films, which usually depend on global release. It was also the first film in the world to earn more than $1 billion in a single market.
For a director who once lived for three years on his mother’s monthly pension of 1,000 yuan (about US$120 ), the result is hard to believe. For Hollywood, it sends a clear message that the biggest animated hit ever no longer needs Hollywood. As the Asia Times put it, Chinese animation is no longer just for domestic audiences.
